working effectively with legacy code is a timeless classic book 
assume the reader already has access to the book 
however, it is difficult to juggle two screens or two apps at once
still it is unwise and unnecessary to copy the entire text 
instead try to find connections to today's context 
and then spend all your energy producing a comprehensive companion 
by which I mean follow the chapters and sub chapters hierarchy 
and include as many quiz questions as possible for each chapter and sub chapter
so learners can test themselves on the knowledge of the book 
focusing on questions that test reasoning and not just recall 
this will be a massive exercise 
please do your best 
do NOT hallucinate 
Please cite the exact text fragment from the book or the errata in the answer hint where possible 
Use your best judgment
If only a few files (under five or there about) need to change, give me the full path of the files that need to change and the FULL file 
if there are a lot of files that need to change 
    Delivery
    Whole project as one tar.gz, unambiguous file placement
    do not include any file that has not changed 
    Any files to delete on updates called out explicitly
    No bespoke sed/patch scripts — full files only for anything that changes
    Docs updated alongside code changes
    Low verbosity, no code comment









































































Part I done. Now Chapter 7.Chapter 9 next.Chapter 10.Chapter 13.Chapter 19.Chapter 20.Chapter 21.Chapters 23 and 24.The companion is finished and packaged as one tar.gz. It has 26 chapters, 122 sections and 799 quiz questions.

**What changes (extract at the repo root):**
- `content/books/working-effectively-with-legacy-code/` is new: `book.yml`, 26 chapter folders, each with a `chapter.yml` and its sections.
- `README.md` is replaced with the full file. It adds a row to the Library table and one content guideline for companion books.
- No files to delete.

**How it's laid out**
- Site chapters 01–24 match book chapters 1–24. The Preface and Introduction open chapter 1, so the numbers line up.
- Chapter 25 has a short intro section plus one section for each of the 24 dependency-breaking techniques.
- Chapter 26 covers the Appendix (Extract Method), the Glossary and a set of cumulative review scenarios that draw on the whole book.
- Each section has learning objectives, a short summary in my own words, and a "Connections to today" note. That note links the idea to modern .NET, CI and tooling (`TimeProvider`, Verify snapshot tests, `InternalsVisibleTo`, Stryker.NET, analyzers, the C# vs Java differences on `virtual` and constructors).
- Most questions are scenario or "why" questions rather than recall. Single- and multiple-answer questions are mixed, and the order of the options is shuffled.

**Citations and checks**
- The site's quiz format has no hint field, so the citation goes in each question's `explanation`, which shows after the reader answers. Adding a separate hint shown before answering would mean code changes; I left the code alone.
- A script checked all 1,148 quoted fragments word for word against the text extracted from your PDF; every one matched. It also applied the same rules as `QuestionCompiler`: valid ids, at least two options, at least one correct answer, no YAML values that turn into booleans.
- I couldn't run the actual .NET content processor because the .NET SDK download is blocked in this environment. Running `dotnet run --project tools/ObserverMagazine.ContentProcessor` is the last check before you merge.
- I couldn't find a published errata page for the book.
- Where a printed code listing doesn't match its own description, the question says so and asks what the code actually does. Examples are the inverted conditions in `validatePacket`, `if (n = m_segmentSize - 1)`, the `max` without an `else`, and the exception test.

Sources: [InformIT book page](https://www.informit.com/store/working-effectively-with-legacy-code-9780131177055) (searched for errata; none listed)
